## Opening {#opening}

Most songs on Spotify never find an audience, not because they are bad, but because the platform is enormous. We analyzed 89,741 tracks with Spotify’s popularity score and nine audio features to ask a simple question: can you hear why some songs reach people and most do not?

The answer is messier than a formula. Read top to bottom and explore the visualizations. If you have your own song you're curious about, try out the [slider panel](#sec-slider) at the end, dial in five audio features, and see where your track would land.

## How popular are most songs, really? {#sec-popularity}

Popularity runs from 0 (almost no streams) to 100 (massive reach). In this dataset, most tracks pile up at the low end. Only a thin slice reaches the top, and a score of 80 or above is very rare.

The chart groups scores into 10-point bands, read from bottom to top. Each bar shows how many tracks fall in that range. Long bars mean many songs, short bars mean few.

Only 3% of tracks score above 70, and 10.5% score exactly zero. The median sits at 33, pulled up by the small number of hits at the top.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from bokeh_story import story_figure_html

display(HTML(story_figure_html("sec1")))
```

::: {.story-takeaway}
Takeaway: Long bars at the bottom mean most tracks are rarely heard. Short bars near the top mean hits are rare.
:::

## Which features are linked to popularity? {#sec-correlations}

Spotify calculates nine audio features for every track. We measured how strongly each one links to popularity, on a scale from 0 (no link) to 1 (perfect link). Features turn out to explain each other far better than they explain popularity.

```{=html}
<details class="story-feature-guide">
  <summary class="story-feature-guide__summary"><span class="story-feature-guide__label">Glossary:</span> What do these audio features actually mean?</summary>
  <div class="story-feature-guide__body">
    <div class="story-feature-grid">
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Danceability</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How well a track works for dancing (tempo, rhythm, beat). 0 = hard to dance to, 1 = made for the floor.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Energy</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How intense and active a song feels. Loud, fast, dense tracks score high; soft acoustic pieces score low.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Valence</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How positive or happy a track sounds. High = cheerful; low = melancholic or dark.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Acousticness</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How likely the track uses only acoustic instruments. Near 1.0 = almost nothing electronic.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Instrumentalness</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How much of a track avoids vocals. Above 0.5 = mostly instrumental; regular singing ≈ 0.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Speechiness</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How much sounds like spoken words. Rap and spoken-word score high; most songs stay below 0.1.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Liveness</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">How likely the track was recorded live. Above 0.8 strongly suggests a concert recording.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Loudness</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">Overall volume in decibels (dB). Typically −60 dB (near silence) to 0 dB (as loud as digital allows).</p>
      </div>
      <div class="story-feature-card">
        <p class="story-feature-card__title">Tempo</p>
        <p class="story-feature-card__desc">Speed in beats per minute (BPM). Ballads ~60–80 BPM; pop and dance often ~120–140 BPM.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</details>
```

None of the nine features strongly predicts popularity. The closest one is instrumentalness, at −0.127. That negative value means tracks with fewer vocals tend to be less popular, which makes sense since most streamed music has singing in it. Loudness and danceability come next, but their links are even weaker. Energy, valence, and tempo show almost no relationship with popularity at all.

What the features do predict is each other. The two strongest pairs are energy and loudness (r = +0.759) and energy and acousticness (r = −0.733). In other words, loud tracks tend to feel intense, and intense tracks tend not to be acoustic. Danceability and valence also move together (r = +0.493), so songs that sound happier are generally easier to dance to. These are real patterns. They just do not transfer to popularity.

The charts below show danceability and energy plotted against popularity, plus the full feature correlation heatmap.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from bokeh_story import story_figure_html

display(HTML(story_figure_html("sec2")))
```

::: {.story-takeaway}
Takeaway: Features explain each other far more than they explain popularity. The heatmap patterns are stronger than any single scatter trend.
:::

## How do genres differ from each other? {#sec-genres}

We picked six genres from the 113 in the dataset: Classical, Hip-Hop, Jazz, Metal, Pop, and Rock. The radar chart shows each genre’s average profile, and the box plot shows how spread out energy is within each genre.

Classical is the most acoustic and calm, Metal the loudest and least acoustic. Hip-Hop leads on danceability, while Pop and Rock sit in the middle on most traits. The dashed overlay in the radar updates when you use the slider panel at the end.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

from IPython.display import HTML, display
from bokeh_story import story_figure_html

display(HTML(story_figure_html("sec3")))
```

::: {.story-takeaway}
Takeaway: Each genre has a distinct shape on the radar. Classical and Metal are near-opposites, while Pop and Rock cluster in the middle on most traits.
:::

## What does a hit actually sound like? {#sec-hits}

We split tracks into the top 10% (hits, score above 60) and the bottom 10% (non-hits, score 0) and compared their average feature values. The differences are patterns, not a recipe. The overlap between the two groups is large.

Hits are louder, more danceable and energetic, and less acoustic. Valence, the measure of how happy a song sounds, is nearly identical between the two groups (0.484 vs 0.483). Sounding happy alone does not make a hit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from bokeh_story import story_figure_html

display(HTML(story_figure_html("sec4")))
```

::: {.story-takeaway}
Takeaway: Hits tend to be louder, more danceable, and less acoustic. But valence barely differs, so sounding happy alone does not make a track popular.
:::

## Where do genres sit on a happy/energetic map? {#sec-moodmap}

Each dot is a genre. Left to right goes from sad to happy (valence), bottom to top from calm to intense (energy). The six focus genres are highlighted and the rest appear as grey dots. Most genres land in the energetic half of the map.

Hip-Hop sits happy and energetic. Metal is intense but emotionally darker. Jazz and Classical cluster calm and low-valence. The star, which represents your slider track, appears here when you try the panel below.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from bokeh_story import story_figure_html

display(HTML(story_figure_html("sec5")))
```

::: {.story-takeaway}
Takeaway: Most genres land in the energetic half of the map. Calm, low-energy styles are a small island compared with everything else.
:::

## Closing {#closing}

No single audio feature reliably predicts popularity. Correlations are real but small, and the overlap between hits and non-hits is enormous.

What the data cannot capture matters too: timing, playlists, algorithms, culture, luck. Most songs stay unheard, a few break through, and audio features are only one piece of that picture.

::: {.story-limitations}
What this story does not claim: a formula for hits, causation from correlation, or live Spotify data. Patterns only.
:::
